skills.name: Counting Objects
skills.target: I can count a group of objects and write the number.
skills.misconception: Skipping or double-counting objects that are not in a line.
skills.support: Touch and move each object as it is counted, or count objects in ten frames.

skills.name: Counting On to 120
skills.target: I can count forward from any number up to 120 and say what number comes next.
skills.misconception: Getting stuck at a decade change (…48, 49, 40) or after 100 (…109, 200).
skills.support: Use a 120 chart: when the ones reach 9, move to the next row and the tens go up by one.

skills.name: Reading and Writing Numbers to 120
skills.target: I can read and write numbers to 120 and match number words to numerals.
skills.misconception: Writing numbers as they sound (one hundred four → 1004) or reversing teen digits (sixteen → 61).
skills.support: Build the number with tens and ones, then write the tens digit first.

skills.name: Counting On and Back to Add and Subtract
skills.target: I can count on to add and count back to subtract.
skills.misconception: Counting the start number as the first jump (5 + 3 → 5, 6, 7).
skills.support: Say the start number, then count only the jumps on a number line.

skills.name: Adding within 10
skills.target: I can add two numbers with a sum up to 10.
skills.misconception: Counting all objects again instead of counting on, and losing track.
skills.support: Put the bigger number in your head and count on the smaller number.

skills.name: Subtracting within 10
skills.target: I can subtract numbers within 10.
skills.misconception: Subtracting the larger number from the smaller one, or adding instead of taking away.
skills.support: Act it out with counters: show the whole, take some away, count what is left.

skills.name: Making Ten
skills.target: I can find the number that goes with another number to make 10.
skills.misconception: Thinking 6 and 3 make ten because the ten frame looks almost full.
skills.support: Fill a ten frame and count the empty boxes.

skills.name: Number Partners within 10
skills.target: I can break a number up to 10 into two parts and find a missing part.
skills.misconception: Adding the whole and the part instead of finding the missing part.
skills.support: Use a part-part-whole mat: cover one part and ask what is hiding.

skills.name: Adding within 20 with Strategies
skills.target: I can add within 20 by making a ten, using doubles, or counting on.
skills.misconception: Counting on from the smaller number and losing count, or forgetting part of the second number after making ten.
skills.support: Fill a ten frame first, then add the leftover counters in a second frame.

skills.name: Subtracting within 20 with Strategies
skills.target: I can subtract within 20 by counting back, going back to 10, or thinking addition.
skills.misconception: Subtracting the smaller ones digit from the larger one (14 − 6 → 12).
skills.support: Ask “6 plus what makes 14?” and jump to 10 first on a number line.

skills.name: Adding in Any Order and Adding Three Numbers
skills.target: I can change the order of addends and add three numbers by finding a ten first.
skills.misconception: Thinking 3 + 8 and 8 + 3 have different answers, or leaving out one of three addends.
skills.support: Turn the domino around; it has the same dots. Circle two addends that make 10.

skills.name: Related Facts and Fact Families
skills.target: I can use an addition fact to solve a related subtraction fact.
skills.misconception: Writing a subtraction fact that starts with a part (6 − 14 = 8).
skills.support: Use a part-part-whole mat: in subtraction the whole comes first.

units.name: The Equal Sign and Missing Numbers

skills.name: True or False Equations
skills.target: I can tell whether an equation is true or false by checking that both sides are the same amount.
skills.misconception: Thinking the equal sign means “the answer comes next,” so 7 = 7 or 5 = 2 + 3 looks wrong.
skills.support: Read = as “is the same as” and build each side with cubes.

skills.name: Finding the Missing Number
skills.target: I can find the unknown number in an addition or subtraction equation.
skills.misconception: Combining all numbers shown (8 + ___ = 11 → 19).
skills.support: Ask what number makes both sides the same; check by putting it in the blank.

skills.name: Balancing Both Sides
skills.target: I can find a number that makes both sides of an equation the same, such as 6 + 4 = 5 + ___.
skills.misconception: Writing the total of the first side in the blank (6 + 4 = 5 + 10).
skills.support: Find the amount on the side you know, then ask what the other side still needs.

skills.name: Add To and Take From Stories
skills.target: I can solve stories where some are added or taken away.
skills.misconception: Adding every pair of numbers in a story without thinking about what happened.
skills.support: Act the story out: did the group get bigger or smaller?

skills.name: Put Together and Take Apart Stories
skills.target: I can solve stories about two parts and a total.
skills.misconception: Adding the total and a part when a part is missing.
skills.support: Draw a part-part-whole picture and label which number is the total.

skills.name: Compare Stories
skills.target: I can solve stories that ask how many more or how many fewer.
skills.misconception: Adding because the word “more” appears in the question.
skills.support: Line up the two groups and count the extra objects.

skills.name: Stories with a Missing Start or Change
skills.target: I can solve stories where the start or the change is unknown.
skills.misconception: Using the last number in the story as the answer, or adding when the start is unknown.
skills.support: Write an equation with a blank in the right place, then find the blank.

skills.name: Stories with Three Numbers
skills.target: I can solve stories that add three numbers with a total up to 20.
skills.misconception: Adding only two of the three numbers.
skills.support: Underline each number in the story and check that all three are added.

skills.name: A Ten Is Ten Ones
skills.target: I can make a ten from ten ones and tell how many tens and ones are in a group.
skills.misconception: Counting a ten rod as one, not ten.
skills.support: Bundle ten straws and count the bundle as “ten.”

skills.name: Teen Numbers
skills.target: I can show a number from 11 to 19 as one ten and some ones.
skills.misconception: Thinking 16 is 6 tens and 1 one, or writing sixteen as 61.
skills.support: Fill one ten frame and put the extra ones in a second frame.

skills.name: Counting by Tens
skills.target: I can count by tens and tell how many tens are in 10, 20, 30, … 90.
skills.misconception: Thinking 50 is 5 ones, or counting by tens as 10, 20, 30, 31.
skills.support: Count ten rods: “1 ten, 10; 2 tens, 20 …”.

skills.name: Tens and Ones in Two-Digit Numbers
skills.target: I can tell how many tens and ones are in a two-digit number and show it with blocks.
skills.misconception: Mixing up the places (47 → 7 tens and 4 ones).
skills.support: Read the tens digit first, then build the rods and cubes to check.

skills.name: Comparing Tens and Ones
skills.target: I can tell which of two numbers is greater by comparing the tens first, then the ones.
skills.misconception: Comparing the ones digits first (29 is greater than 41 because 9 > 1).
skills.support: Build both numbers with blocks; the number with more tens is greater.

skills.name: Using >, =, and <
skills.target: I can write a comparison using the symbols >, =, and <.
skills.misconception: Pointing the symbol the wrong way.
skills.support: The open side of the symbol faces the greater number.

skills.name: Reasoning about Comparisons
skills.target: I can find numbers that make a comparison true and explain my thinking.
skills.misconception: Thinking a number with a bigger ones digit is always greater.
skills.support: Check the tens digits first and use a number line to see which number comes later.

skills.name: 10 More and 10 Less
skills.target: I can find 10 more or 10 less than a two-digit number without counting by ones.
skills.misconception: Changing the ones digit instead of the tens digit (34 + 10 → 35).
skills.support: Add or take away one ten rod: only the tens digit changes.

skills.name: Adding and Subtracting Tens
skills.target: I can add tens to a two-digit number and subtract tens from tens.
skills.misconception: Adding the tens to the ones (40 + 23 → 27), or writing 50 − 20 = 3.
skills.support: Think in tens: 5 tens − 2 tens = 3 tens, which is 30.

skills.name: Adding a Two-Digit and a One-Digit Number
skills.target: I can add a one-digit number to a two-digit number when no new ten is made.
skills.misconception: Adding the one-digit number to the tens (32 + 5 → 82).
skills.support: Add ones to ones and keep the tens.

skills.name: Making a New Ten
skills.target: I can add a one-digit number to a two-digit number when the ones make a new ten.
skills.misconception: Writing the ones sum as a digit (38 + 5 → 313).
skills.support: Fill the ten first: 38 + 2 = 40, then add the 3 left.

skills.name: Adding Two-Digit Numbers with Models
skills.target: I can add two two-digit numbers within 100 by adding tens and tens and ones and ones.
skills.misconception: Adding a tens digit to a ones digit.
skills.support: Draw tens as lines and ones as dots; add each kind separately.

skills.name: Comparing and Ordering Lengths
skills.target: I can compare two lengths and put three objects in order from shortest to longest.
skills.misconception: Comparing objects that do not start at the same line.
skills.support: Line up the ends before comparing.

skills.name: Comparing Lengths Indirectly
skills.target: I can use a third object to compare two lengths.
skills.misconception: Thinking a comparison cannot be made without putting the two objects side by side.
skills.support: If the rug is longer than the string and the string is longer than the desk, the rug is longer than the desk.

skills.name: Measuring with Length Units
skills.target: I can measure a length by counting same-size units laid end to end.
skills.misconception: Counting the spaces or lines instead of the units.
skills.support: Count each cube or paper clip as you touch it.

skills.name: Measuring Correctly
skills.target: I can tell when a measurement is wrong because of gaps, overlaps, or units of different sizes.
skills.misconception: Leaving gaps or overlaps, or mixing big and small units.
skills.support: Check that units touch end to end and are all the same size.

skills.name: Time to the Hour
skills.target: I can tell and write time to the hour on analog and digital clocks.
skills.misconception: Mixing up the hour hand and the minute hand.
skills.support: The short hand tells the hour; the long hand points to 12 at o'clock.

skills.name: Time to the Half Hour
skills.target: I can tell and write time to the half hour on analog and digital clocks.
skills.misconception: Reading the next hour at half past (the hour hand is past 3, so it says 4:30).
skills.support: At half past, the hour hand is halfway between two numbers; read the number it has passed.

skills.name: Matching and Using Clock Times
skills.target: I can match analog and digital times and tell what time it will be one hour or half an hour later.
skills.misconception: Writing half past 6 as 6:50 or 6:3.
skills.support: Half past means 30 minutes; the long hand points to 6.

skills.name: Sorting and Tally Marks
skills.target: I can sort objects into up to three groups and use tally marks to show how many.
skills.misconception: Counting each bundle of five tally marks as one.
skills.support: Count tally bundles by fives, then count on by ones.

skills.name: Reading Picture Graphs and Tables
skills.target: I can read how many are in each category of a picture graph, tally chart, or table.
skills.misconception: Reading the wrong row or counting the label.
skills.support: Point to the category name, then slide across the row.

skills.name: Answering Questions about Data
skills.target: I can find the total and tell how many more or fewer are in one category than another.
skills.misconception: Adding when the question asks how many more.
skills.support: Find the two numbers first, then decide: in all means add; how many more means compare.

skills.name: Defining Attributes of Shapes
skills.target: I can tell which attributes make a shape what it is (closed, number of sides and corners) and which do not (color, size, position).
skills.misconception: Thinking a turned square is not a square, or that color or size changes a shape's name.
skills.support: Turn and resize paper shapes; count sides and corners again.

skills.name: Naming Two- and Three-Dimensional Shapes
skills.target: I can name circles, triangles, squares, rectangles, trapezoids, hexagons, cubes, cones, cylinders, and rectangular prisms.
skills.misconception: Calling every four-sided shape a square, or calling a cylinder a circle.
skills.support: Count sides and corners; for solids, look for flat faces and curved surfaces.

skills.name: Composing Shapes
skills.target: I can put shapes together to make new shapes and tell how many shapes I used.
skills.misconception: Thinking a new shape cannot be made from smaller pieces, or counting outlines instead of pieces.
skills.support: Use pattern blocks to cover a shape and count the pieces.

skills.name: Halves and Fourths
skills.target: I can split circles and rectangles into 2 or 4 equal shares and name halves, fourths, and quarters.
skills.misconception: Calling unequal parts halves or fourths.
skills.support: Fold paper shapes so the parts match exactly.

skills.name: More Shares Are Smaller Shares
skills.target: I can describe a whole as two halves or four fourths and explain that more equal shares are smaller shares.
skills.misconception: Thinking a fourth is bigger than a half because 4 is bigger than 2.
skills.support: Cut two same-size paper strips into halves and fourths and compare the pieces.
